code.title: N+1 queries versus one JOIN
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE author(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE book(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, author_id INT, title TEXT);
INSERT INTO author VALUES (1,'Ann'),(2,'Bo'),(3,'Cy');
INSERT INTO book VALUES (1,1,'A1'),(2,1,'A2'),(3,2,'B1'),(4,3,'C1'),(5,3,'C2');
""")

count = 0
def on_sql(stmt):          # called for every statement the driver executes
    global count
    count += 1
db.set_trace_callback(on_sql)

# N+1: one query for authors, then one query per author
count = 0
result = {}
for aid, name in db.execute("SELECT id, name FROM author").fetchall():
    rows = db.execute("SELECT title FROM book WHERE author_id=?", (aid,)).fetchall()
    result[name] = [r[0] for r in rows]
print("N+1  :", result, "queries =", count)

# Fix: one JOIN, grouped in memory (2 queries in total would also be fine)
count = 0
result = {}
for name, title in db.execute(
        "SELECT a.name, b.title FROM author a JOIN book b ON b.author_id=a.id ORDER BY a.id, b.id"):
    result.setdefault(name, []).append(title)
print("JOIN :", result, "queries =", count)
# Cost: N+1 grows with authors (1+N round trips); the JOIN stays at 1.

followUps:
Because the database must join, then page, and paging cuts the result in the middle of a parent's children. With a collection join, each parent appears once per child row. If 10 orders have 5 items each, the join returns 50 rows, and LIMIT 20 returns 20 of those rows, which could be 4 orders with half of the last one's items missing.

Hibernate cannot trust that, so it loads all rows and pages in memory (warning HHH000104 in Hibernate 5, HHH90003004 in Hibernate 6). That can mean millions of rows. Fix: page the parent IDs first, then fetch their children with WHERE id IN (:ids) or use batch fetching.

Make the test fail when the number of queries is higher than expected. Wrap the DataSource with a counting proxy (datasource-proxy or Hibernate Statistics) and assert the count for each important endpoint after a request.

Example: the list endpoint with 20 rows must run at most 3 queries. If someone adds a lazy association, the count becomes 23 and CI fails. Seed at least 2 to 3 parents so a loop shows up as a count that grows. Also run with SQL logging and check slow-query and repeated-statement reports in staging.

assertThat(queryCount()).isLessThanOrEqualTo(3);

Load what you need while the session is still open; do not widen the session to hide the problem. Fetch the data inside the service method (join fetch, entity graph, or a DTO projection) and return plain DTOs to the controller.

Bad fixes: switching the relation to EAGER everywhere, or enabling Open Session In View. Good fix example: @EntityGraph(attributePaths="items") on the repository method that the screen uses, or a query that selects only the 4 columns the response needs. The transaction boundary then decides what is loaded, and nothing lazy escapes it.

Open Session In View keeps the Hibernate session open for the whole web request, so lazy fields still work in the controller and the view. Many teams switch it off (spring.jpa.open-in-view=false) because it hides N+1 queries and holds a database connection until the response is written.

If a request spends 200 ms rendering JSON and 50 ms in the database, the connection is busy for 250 ms, so the pool runs dry sooner. It also lets queries run from the view layer, outside any transaction rules. Turning it off forces you to fetch data deliberately in the service layer.

Total connections grow with the pod count, so 50 pods multiply the pool size by 50, and the database may refuse the extras. With a pool of 20 per pod, 50 pods ask for 1,000 connections, while PostgreSQL often defaults to 100 max_connections.

Fix: shrink each pod's pool (for example 4 to 5, so 50 x 5 = 250 at most), then put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front so many app connections share a few real ones (say 100). Also check that the total stays below max_connections minus reserve for admin and other services, and cut hold time first.

Watch the numbers that show waiting, not just size. Key Hikari metrics: hikaricp_connections_active (in use), pending (threads waiting), acquire time (how long a thread waited for a connection), usage time (how long it kept one), and timeout count.

Healthy: pending near 0 and acquire time in single-digit milliseconds. If pending stays above 0 while active equals max, the pool is saturated. If usage time is long, queries or open transactions are the cause. Alert on pending greater than 0 for a minute, and on any timeout.

Turn on leak detection and read the stack trace it prints. Set leakDetectionThreshold (for example 20000 ms): if a connection stays out longer than that, Hikari logs a warning with the stack trace of the code that borrowed it.

Also look at the database: SELECT pid, state, now()-xact_start FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state='idle in transaction' shows sessions that did work and then sat holding a connection. Common causes: a missing try-with-resources, a remote HTTP call inside a transaction, or a batch job that never commits. Active staying at max with no traffic is the usual symptom of a leak.

A shorter timeout makes the app fail fast instead of piling up. The default is 30 seconds, but a user-facing request rarely waits that long, so 30 waiting threads just hold Tomcat workers and the whole service stalls.

If the pool is full, answering in 1 to 3 seconds with an error (or a 503) gives the caller a chance to retry another pod, and keeps threads free. Pick a value a bit below the caller's own timeout. A long connectionTimeout does not create connections; it only delays the failure and hides the overload.

One pod gets the lock and migrates; the others wait or fail safely, as long as you use the tool's lock. Flyway takes a lock on flyway_schema_history (or an advisory lock on PostgreSQL), and Liquibase uses its own DATABASECHANGELOGLOCK table.

The first instance runs migration V12, the second blocks and then sees V12 as already applied. Problems arise if a migration is long: pods may fail health checks and restart. Safer option: run migrations as a separate job or init step before the rollout, then start the app pods with validation only.

Because Hibernate then changes the schema by guessing from your entity classes, with no review, no history and no rollback. ddl-auto=update only adds things: it never drops or renames columns, never migrates data, and behaves differently per database.

Example: rename field name to fullName and Hibernate adds a new empty column, leaving the old data behind. It can also take heavy locks at startup in production. Use validate or none in production and let Flyway or Liquibase own the schema, with versioned scripts that you review.

A trigger copies each write on the old column or table to the new one inside the database, so the data stays in sync even for writers that do not run your new code. It is useful when you cannot change every writer at once (old app versions, batch jobs, other services).

Example: renaming phone to mobile: add the column, add a trigger that sets NEW.mobile = NEW.phone on insert and update, backfill old rows, then switch reads. Downside: triggers are hidden logic and add write cost, so drop the trigger in the contract step.

Without transactional DDL, a failed migration can leave the schema half changed, so keep each migration to one small, repeatable step and plan to roll forward. MySQL commits implicitly after each DDL statement, so a rollback is not possible.

Practical steps: one change per script, write it so it can be rerun (check information_schema first), and test it on a copy. For big tables use online tools such as gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change (or ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE where supported). Take a backup first and keep the expand and contract steps in separate releases.

code.title: Offset vs keyset paging when a row is inserted
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE post(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, ts INT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO post VALUES (?,?)", [(i, 100 + i) for i in range(1, 11)])
db.execute("CREATE INDEX ix ON post(ts DESC, id DESC)")

def ids(rows):
    return [r[0] for r in rows]

# Offset paging: page 1, then a new post arrives, then page 2
p1 = ids(db.execute("SELECT id FROM post ORDER BY ts DESC, id DESC LIMIT 3 OFFSET 0"))
db.execute("INSERT INTO post VALUES (11, 111)")      # newest row shifts everything down
p2 = ids(db.execute("SELECT id FROM post ORDER BY ts DESC, id DESC LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3"))
print("offset page1", p1, "page2", p2, "(id 8 is repeated)")

# Keyset paging: remember the last (ts, id) of the previous page
db.execute("DELETE FROM post WHERE id=11")
rows = db.execute("SELECT id, ts FROM post ORDER BY ts DESC, id DESC LIMIT 3").fetchall()
print("keyset page1", ids(rows))
last_id, last_ts = rows[-1]
db.execute("INSERT INTO post VALUES (11, 111)")      # same new post arrives
rows = db.execute(
    "SELECT id, ts FROM post WHERE (ts, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY ts DESC, id DESC LIMIT 3",
    (last_ts, last_id)).fetchall()
print("keyset page2", ids(rows), "(no repeat)")
# Keyset cost is O(log n + page) with the index; offset reads and drops OFFSET rows.

followUps:
You keep the last row you showed, and for the previous page you run the same query backwards and then flip the result. For "next" you use (ts, id) < (:ts, :id) ORDER BY ts DESC, id DESC. For "previous" you use (ts, id) > (:first_ts, :first_id) ORDER BY ts ASC, id ASC LIMIT n, then reverse the n rows in code.

Return two cursors with each page: one built from the first row and one from the last. The index can be read in either direction, so both are cheap. Example: page 2 shows ids 7,6,5; previous query returns 8,9,10 ascending, which you reverse to 10,9,8.

Allow only a fixed list of sort columns, and put the chosen column plus the unique id into the cursor. Never put the column name straight into SQL from the request; map it from a whitelist such as created or price.

Each sort needs its own composite index, (price, id) for example, so offer only a few. The cursor stores the sort name and the last values, and a cursor made for one sort is rejected for another. If a column can be NULL or changes often, either exclude it or sort by COALESCE(col, 0) in an expression index. Users who need any column with page jumps should be given offset on small result sets.

code.title: Keyset paging bug: missing tie-breaker
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE ev(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, ts INT)")
# Rows 4,5,6,7 share the same timestamp
db.executemany("INSERT INTO ev VALUES (?,?)",
               [(1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 30), (4, 40), (5, 40), (6, 40), (7, 40), (8, 50)])

def page_bad(last_ts):             # bug: bookmark is only ts
    sql = "SELECT id, ts FROM ev WHERE ts < ? ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 3"
    return db.execute(sql, (last_ts,)).fetchall()

def page_good(last):               # fix: total order (ts, id) and strict compare
    sql = ("SELECT id, ts FROM ev WHERE (ts, id) < (?, ?) "
           "ORDER BY ts DESC, id DESC LIMIT 3")
    return db.execute(sql, last).fetchall()

first = db.execute("SELECT id, ts FROM ev ORDER BY ts DESC, id DESC LIMIT 3").fetchall()
print("page 1       :", [r[0] for r in first])      # 8, 7, 6
print("bad page 2   :", [r[0] for r in page_bad(first[-1][1])])   # skips 5 and 4
print("good page 2  :", [r[0] for r in page_good((first[-1][1], first[-1][0]))])

followUps:
PostgreSQL treats NULL as larger than any value, so in ascending order NULLs come last and in descending order they come first. SQLite treats NULL as smaller, so ascending puts them first.

That means the same query gives a different page order on each, and a keyset comparison like ts < :x never matches NULL rows (the result is unknown), so those rows vanish from paging. Be explicit with ORDER BY ts DESC NULLS LAST (PostgreSQL, recent SQLite) or avoid NULL in sort keys with a default value or COALESCE in a matching expression index.

Then rows can move across the bookmark between requests and be skipped or shown twice, so prefer a key that never changes. Good keys: a creation time and id. Bad keys: updated_at or a score.

Example: you sort by updated_at DESC; page 1 ends at 10:00; a row on page 3 is edited and jumps to 10:05, which is before the bookmark in the list, so you never see it. Options: use an immutable key, take a snapshot (repeatable read or a snapshot timestamp in the cursor), or accept it and document that edits can reorder the feed. Feeds usually accept this.

code.title: Optimistic locking with a version column
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE item(id INT PRIMARY KEY, qty INT, version INT)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO item VALUES (1, 10, 1)")

def read():
    return db.execute("SELECT qty, version FROM item WHERE id=1").fetchone()

def save(new_qty, seen_version):
    # The version check is part of the WHERE clause, so the update is atomic
    cur = db.execute(
        "UPDATE item SET qty=?, version=version+1 WHERE id=1 AND version=?",
        (new_qty, seen_version))
    return cur.rowcount == 1       # 0 rows means someone else saved first

# Two users open the same form
qty_a, ver_a = read()
qty_b, ver_b = read()
print("A saves qty 8 :", save(qty_a - 2, ver_a))
print("B saves qty 7 :", save(qty_b - 3, ver_b), "(conflict, B must reload)")
# B retries with fresh data
qty_b, ver_b = read()
print("B retry       :", save(qty_b - 3, ver_b))
print("final         :", read())     # (5, 3)

followUps:
It adds a version column and checks it on every write; the UPDATE only succeeds if the version is still the one you read. With @Version, Hibernate runs UPDATE ... SET qty=?, version=version+1 WHERE id=? AND version=?.

If zero rows were updated, it throws OptimisticLockException, and you reload and retry or return 409. Example: two users load version 3; the first saves and makes it 4; the second tries to save with version 3 and fails. It also works across requests when you send the version back in a form or ETag.

Make two transactions read the same row and then both write it, and assert that exactly one succeeds. Use two threads and a latch or barrier so both read before either writes, which is repeatable instead of timing luck.

load(1) in tx A and tx B (both version 1)
A.save() -> ok
B.save() -> expect OptimisticLockException
assert version == 2 and no data lost

Run it against the real database (Testcontainers), not an in-memory fake, and also test the retry path ends with both changes applied.

code.title: Lost update vs atomic UPDATE
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE acct(id INT PRIMARY KEY, balance INT)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO acct VALUES (1, 100)")

def balance():
    return db.execute("SELECT balance FROM acct WHERE id=1").fetchone()[0]

# Lost update: both transactions read first, then both write a computed value
read_a = balance()
read_b = balance()
db.execute("UPDATE acct SET balance=? WHERE id=1", (read_a - 30,))
db.execute("UPDATE acct SET balance=? WHERE id=1", (read_b - 50,))   # overwrites A
print("read-modify-write:", balance(), "(should be 20)")

# Fix: let the database do the arithmetic in one atomic statement
db.execute("UPDATE acct SET balance=100 WHERE id=1")
for amount in (30, 50):
    cur = db.execute(
        "UPDATE acct SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id=1 AND balance >= ?",
        (amount, amount))        # the guard refuses overdrafts
    print("withdraw", amount, "ok" if cur.rowcount else "refused")
print("atomic update    :", balance())

followUps:
READ COMMITTED lets a transaction see changes other transactions committed while it runs, so a lost update, a non-repeatable read and a phantom row are all possible. It only prevents dirty reads (seeing uncommitted data).

Example: A reads balance 100, B commits balance 70, A then writes 100-30=70 from its stale read. Nothing stops it, and B's change is lost. That is why plain read-then-write needs an atomic UPDATE, a version check or FOR UPDATE. PostgreSQL's default is READ COMMITTED, and so is the default in most others (MySQL InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ).

You cannot share a row lock across services, so you use a single owner for each record or a version check at the one place that stores it. The ideas are the same: conditional writes (compare-and-set on a version), idempotency keys, and one writer per key.

Examples: DynamoDB conditional writes attribute_not_exists or a version attribute; a partitioned queue so one consumer handles all events of one account in order; sagas with compensating steps for work across services. Distributed locks (Redis, ZooKeeper) are a last resort because leases can expire while the holder is still working, so pair them with a fencing token.

code.title: Deadlock from lock order, fixed by sorting

followUps:
NOWAIT makes the query fail at once if the row is already locked, instead of waiting. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT raises an error immediately, so a transaction can never sit in a wait cycle.

Use it when you would rather tell the user "someone else is editing this" or retry later than block a thread. Related options: SKIP LOCKED skips locked rows (good for job queues) and lock_timeout waits for a limited time such as 2 seconds. None remove the need for a consistent lock order, but they turn a possible hang into a quick, handled error.

Gap locks are InnoDB locks on the empty space between index records, which stop other transactions from inserting into that range. Under REPEATABLE READ, a locking read like SELECT ... WHERE id BETWEEN 10 AND 20 FOR UPDATE locks the range, not just existing rows.

Deadlock example: two transactions each take a gap lock on the same gap (gap locks do not conflict with each other), then both try to insert into it and each waits for the other. Reduce the risk by locking by unique key, keeping transactions short, or using READ COMMITTED (which uses few gap locks) if your application can accept that.

It means a user must see their own changes even if the replica has not received them yet, and also never see time go backwards. Monotonic reads is the second part: once you saw data at some point, later reads never show older data.

Failure example: you refresh a page, replica A (current) shows 5 comments, the next refresh hits replica B (lagging) and shows 3. Fix: pin a user's reads to one replica (hash of user id or session), or send them to the primary when their session has recent writes, or require the replica's replay position to be at least the user's last write position.

Create lag on purpose and check the pages that read right after a write. Options: pause replication on a staging replica (pg_wal_replay_pause() on PostgreSQL), add network delay with a tool such as tc/toxiproxy, or use a fake router that delays replica reads by a few seconds.

Then run the flows: create an item and open its page, edit a profile and reload, log in and check permissions. Assert the user sees the new data (via primary fallback) and that the app falls back to the primary when lag is over a threshold, say 5 seconds. Also test that lag metrics and alerts fire.

Shard when writes or data size no longer fit on one primary, not when reads are high. Replicas scale reads; they do nothing for writes, since every write still goes to the one primary and is copied to each replica.

Signs you need sharding: primary CPU or IOPS is high from writes, the working set exceeds memory, or the table is too large to maintain (vacuum, backups, migrations take too long). Example: 95% reads at 70% CPU: add replicas and caching. 60% writes at 90% CPU with 5 TB: partition first, then shard by tenant or user id. Sharding costs cross-shard queries and transactions, so do it last.

Compare before and after with the same load test and real metrics, not a feeling. Pick targets first, such as p95 latency 200 ms and database CPU under 60% at 2x today's traffic.

Steps: record a baseline (p50, p95, p99, queries per request, CPU, pool pending); change one thing at a time; replay production-like traffic (captured queries or a traffic mirror); then compare. For caches also watch hit rate (say above 90%) and for replicas lag and fallback rate. Keep the change only if the numbers move, and keep the dashboards for regressions.

The connection pool graph: active versus max, with pending threads and acquire time. If pending is above 0 while database CPU is low, the app is waiting for a connection, not for a query to compute.

This is the fastest split between app-side waiting and database-side work. Next in order: transaction duration (long ones hold connections), lock waits in the database, then the trace for query count per request. If the pool graph is flat and healthy, move on to network latency and replica lag.

Recreate the shape of production: similar data volume, the same pool size and a load test with realistic concurrency. A tiny staging database hides the problem because every query is fast and nobody waits.

Steps: load a copy of production-sized data (anonymised), set the pool to the production value, run the new endpoint at production request rate (k6 or Gatling), and watch pending, query count and lock waits. Add artificial network latency of 1 to 2 ms to the database, since N+1 and chatty code hurt only when each round trip costs time. Compare traces with the old release.
